punic-people.name: Punic people
punic-people.summary: The Carthaginians, a Semitic people who migrated from Phoenicia to the western Mediterranean in the Early Iron Age, founding Carthage and some 300 other settlements from North Africa to Spain.

muslim-conquest-of-the-maghreb.name: Muslim conquest of the Maghreb
muslim-conquest-of-the-maghreb.summary: Nearly 70-year campaign (647-709) in which the Rashidun and Umayyad Caliphates conquered Byzantine North Africa, ending Byzantine rule in the Maghreb under Caliph al-Walid I.

tajine-zitoun.name: Tajine Zitoun
tajine-zitoun.summary: A traditional Algerian stew from Algiers, cooked in an earthenware tajine pot with meat such as lamb, turkey or chicken and olives.

diodorus-siculus.name: Diodorus Siculus
diodorus-siculus.summary: Ancient Greek historian from Sicily (1st century BC) who wrote the 40-book universal history Bibliotheca historica, covering world history up to about 60 BC.

bes.name: Bes
bes.summary: Ancient Egyptian deity of Nubian origin, worshipped as protector of households, mothers, children and childbirth; his worship spread from Syria to Spain and into the Roman and Achaemenid empires.

julius-caesar.name: Julius Caesar
julius-caesar.summary: Roman general and statesman, 100 to 44 BC, who became dictator of the Republic, expanded Roman territory through the Gallic Wars, and was assassinated in 44 BC.

roman-carthage.name: Roman Carthage
roman-carthage.summary: City rebuilt on the site of destroyed Punic Carthage from 49 to 44 BC under Julius Caesar, growing into one of the largest cities of the Roman Empire and center of its African province.

isis.name: Isis
isis.summary: A major ancient Egyptian goddess, first recorded in the Old Kingdom, who resurrected her husband Osiris and protected their son Horus; her worship later spread across the Greco-Roman world.

ren-dussaud.name: René Dussaud
ren-dussaud.summary: A French archaeologist and Orientalist (1868–1958) who led French excavations in the Middle East and became curator of Near Eastern Antiquities at the Louvre.

victor-vitensis.name: Victor Vitensis
victor-vitensis.summary: 5th-century African bishop of Byzacena, remembered for his history of the Vandal persecution of Christians under kings Genseric and Huneric.

vandals.name: Vandals
vandals.summary: A Germanic people who conquered Roman North Africa and ruled it for a century, sacking Rome in 455, until the Byzantine Empire defeated them in 534.

cyprian.name: Cyprian
cyprian.summary: Bishop of Carthage and early Christian writer of Berber descent (c. 210–258 AD), whose skilled Latin rhetoric and eventual martyrdom made him a leading figure of Western Christianity.

tertullian.name: Tertullian
tertullian.summary: Early Christian author and apologist from Carthage, active around 155 to 220 AD; the first to write Christian theology in Latin and to use the term 'trinity'.

battle-of-zama.name: Battle of Zama
battle-of-zama.summary: A battle fought in 202 BC in modern Tunisia, in which Scipio Africanus's Roman army defeated Hannibal's Carthaginians despite their war elephants, ending the Second Punic War and forcing Hannibal into exile.

scipio-africanus.name: Scipio Africanus
scipio-africanus.summary: Roman general (236/235-c.183 BC) who defeated Hannibal at the Battle of Zama in 202 BC, ending the Second Punic War and earning him the epithet 'Africanus'.

hannibal.name: Hannibal
hannibal.summary: A Carthaginian general (247–183/181 BC) who led forces against Rome in the Second Punic War, famously crossing the Alps with war elephants to invade Italy.

utica-tunisia.name: Utica
utica-tunisia.summary: An ancient Phoenician and Carthaginian city near Carthage in modern Tunisia that became an important Roman colony after Carthage's defeat, before its harbour silted up.

mercenary-war.name: Mercenary War
mercenary-war.summary: A mutiny by Carthage's unpaid mercenary troops and rebelling African subjects after the First Punic War (241 to 238/237 BC), eventually suppressed by Carthage.

spendius.name: Spendius
spendius.summary: A former Roman slave who co-led a rebel army against Carthage in the Mercenary War (241 to 238 BC) after Carthage tried to underpay its soldiers.

masinissa.name: Masinissa
masinissa.summary: Numidian king (c. 238–148 BCE) who united the Numidian tribes into a kingdom, allied with Rome, and played a key role at the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE.

numidia.name: Numidia
numidia.summary: An ancient Berber kingdom in what is now Algeria and parts of Tunisia and Libya, unified by King Masinissa during the Second Punic War and later a Roman client state.

battle-of-oroscopa.name: Battle of Oroscopa
battle-of-oroscopa.summary: A 151 BC battle in what is now Tunisia in which Numidia's King Masinissa starved and defeated a Carthaginian army under Hasdrubal, whose surrendering troops were then attacked despite the terms of surrender.

scipio-aemilianus.name: Scipio Aemilianus
scipio-aemilianus.summary: Roman general and statesman (185-129 BC) who destroyed Carthage in the Third Punic War and later fought in Spain's Numantine War; patron of writers including the historian Polybius.

hamilcar-barca.name: Hamilcar Barca
hamilcar-barca.summary: Carthaginian general and statesman (c. 275-228 BC) and father of Hannibal, who fought in the First Punic War and later expanded Carthaginian territory in Spain.

autaritus.name: Autaritus
autaritus.summary: Leader of Gallic mercenaries in the Carthaginian army during the First Punic War, later a rebel commander in the Mercenary War, known for inciting brutality against captives before his death in 238 BCE.

polybius.name: Polybius
polybius.summary: A Greek historian, about 200 to 118 BC, whose Histories chronicled Rome's rise to dominance from 264 to 146 BC; his ideas on checks and balances later influenced the framers of the US Constitution.

hanno-the-navigator.name: Hanno the Navigator
hanno-the-navigator.summary: A Carthaginian explorer of the 5th century BC known for a naval expedition along West Africa's coast, described in an account (periplus) that may show him reaching as far as modern Gabon.

plautus.name: Plautus
plautus.summary: A Roman playwright (c. 254–184 BC) whose comedies are the earliest complete Latin literary works to survive, later influencing Shakespeare and Molière.

poenulus.name: Poenulus
poenulus.summary: A Latin comedy by Plautus, written around 195–189 BC, notable for containing lines of the Punic language spoken by a sympathetically drawn Carthaginian character.

terence.name: Terence
terence.summary: A playwright of the Roman Republic, born around 195 to 185 BC in Carthage and brought to Rome as a slave, whose six surviving comedies remained standard school texts into the 19th century.

scipionic-circle.name: Scipionic Circle
scipionic-circle.summary: Circle of philosophers, poets and politicians patronized by Scipio Aemilianus, favoring Greek culture and a more humane Roman policy; its unity as a real group is doubted by modern scholars.

juba-ii.name: Juba II
juba-ii.summary: Client king of Numidia and then Mauretania (25 BC–AD 23), son of Juba I; also a respected scholar and author, married to Cleopatra's daughter Cleopatra Selene II.

cleopatra.name: Cleopatra
cleopatra.summary: Last active Hellenistic pharaoh, ruling Ptolemaic Egypt from 51 to 30 BC; her death marked Egypt becoming a Roman province and the end of the Hellenistic period.

virgil.name: Virgil
virgil.summary: Ancient Roman poet (70–19 BC) of the Augustan age who wrote the Eclogues, the Georgics and the epic Aeneid, becoming a hugely influential model for later Western literature.

aeneid.name: Aeneid
aeneid.summary: Latin epic poem by Virgil, written between 29 and 19 BC, telling of Aeneas's journey from Troy to Italy and his role as ancestor of the Romans.

dido.name: Dido
dido.summary: Legendary founder and first queen of Carthage in Greek and Roman mythology, best known from Virgil's Aeneid, where she falls in love with Aeneas and kills herself after he leaves; her historicity is uncertain.

aeneas.name: Aeneas
aeneas.summary: Trojan hero of Greco-Roman mythology, son of Anchises and Aphrodite, later cast in Virgil's Aeneid as an ancestor of Rome.

pliny-the-elder.name: Pliny the Elder
pliny-the-elder.summary: A Roman author, naturalist and military commander (23/24–79 AD) who wrote the 37-volume encyclopedia Natural History and died attempting to rescue people during the eruption of Vesuvius.

hiempsal-ii.name: Hiempsal II
hiempsal-ii.summary: King of Numidia from 88 to 60 BC, son of Gauda, half-brother of Jugurtha, and father of Juba I.

timaeus-historian.name: Timaeus of Tauromenium
timaeus-historian.summary: Ancient Greek historian (c. 356/350–260 BC) regarded as the leading authority on the history of the Greek West for centuries.

livy.name: Livy
livy.summary: A Roman historian (59 BC-AD 17) who wrote a monumental history of Rome, Ab Urbe Condita, from its legendary founding through Augustus's reign, and was a friend of Augustus.

temple-of-juno-lacinia-crotone.name: Temple of Hera Lacinia
temple-of-juno-lacinia-crotone.summary: A ruined ancient Greek temple to Hera on a promontory near Crotone in southern Italy, of which a single tall Doric column still stands.

gnaeus-naevius.name: Gnaeus Naevius
gnaeus-naevius.summary: Roman epic poet and dramatist (c. 270-201 BC) who fought in the Punic Wars, invented a new genre of tragedy on Roman themes, and was eventually exiled after satirizing a powerful family.

baths-of-antoninus.name: Baths of Antoninus
baths-of-antoninus.summary: The largest Roman bathhouse complex built in Africa, constructed at Carthage and named for Emperor Antoninus Pius, in use until Vandals destroyed it in 439 CE.

hadrian.name: Hadrian
hadrian.summary: Roman emperor from 117 to 138, born in Hispania, who abandoned Trajan's territorial expansion in favor of stable borders and personally visited almost every province of the empire.

antoninus-pius.name: Antoninus Pius
antoninus-pius.summary: Roman emperor from 138 to 161 CE, one of the Five Good Emperors, whose peaceful reign saw the construction of the Antonine Wall in Scotland.

eratosthenes.name: Eratosthenes
eratosthenes.summary: Ancient Greek polymath (c. 276–c. 195 BC) and chief librarian at Alexandria, first known to calculate Earth's circumference and axial tilt, and founder of scientific chronology and geography as a field.

cyrene-libya.name: Cyrene
cyrene-libya.summary: Ancient Greek colony and Roman city in northeastern Libya, probably settled from Thera in the late seventh century BC. It gave the region the name Cyrenaica and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1982.

apuleius.name: Apuleius
apuleius.summary: Latin prose writer, Platonist philosopher and rhetorician born around 124 in Numidia. He is best known for the novel The Golden Ass, the only ancient Latin novel to survive complete.

madauros.name: Madauros
madauros.summary: Roman-Berber city in Numidia, in present-day Algeria. Its university is often considered one of the earliest centers of higher learning in Africa, dating to the Roman era.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (384–322 BC) who founded the Peripatetic school, tutored Alexander the Great, and laid groundwork for modern science.

hippocrates.name: Hippocrates
hippocrates.summary: A Greek physician and philosopher (c. 460–370 BC) traditionally called the 'Father of Medicine' for pioneering prognosis and clinical observation, and credited with the Hippocratic Oath.

silphium.name: Silphium
silphium.summary: Unidentified plant of classical antiquity used as a seasoning, perfume and medicine. Its resin was so valuable that Cyrene's coins bore its image, and it was said to have died out in Roman times.

zaghouan.name: Zaghouan
zaghouan.summary: A town in northern Tunisia on the Dorsale Mountains, source of the Roman aqueduct that carried water over 100 km to Carthage.

cassius-dionysius.name: Cassius Dionysius
cassius-dionysius.summary: Greek agricultural writer from Utica in the first century BC, probably a freed slave. His farming manual Georgika, in twenty books and now lost, was dedicated to the Roman praetor Sextilius.

diophanes-of-nicaea.name: Diophanes of Nicaea
diophanes-of-nicaea.summary: Greek agricultural writer of the 1st century BC from Nicaea in Bithynia. His abridged farming manual, dedicated to King Deiotarus, was more popular than the original, but both are now lost.

philistus.name: Philistus
philistus.summary: Greek historian from Sicily who lived c. 432 to 356 BC.

tyre-lebanon.name: Tyre
tyre-lebanon.summary: Ancient Phoenician city in modern Lebanon, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and the legendary birthplace of Carthage's founder, Dido.

neo-assyrian-empire.name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
neo-assyrian-empire.summary: An ancient Mesopotamian empire beginning in 911 BCE that grew to dominate the Near East, Egypt and parts of Anatolia, described as history's first world empire.

mauretania.name: Mauretania
mauretania.summary: The Latin name for an ancient region of the Maghreb, in present-day Morocco and Algeria, that became a Roman client kingdom in 25 BCE before being annexed as a province.

mauretania-caesariensis.name: Mauretania Caesariensis
mauretania-caesariensis.summary: A Roman province in present-day Algeria, formed around 42 CE when the Kingdom of Mauretania was divided, named for its capital Caesarea.

mauretania-tingitana.name: Mauretania Tingitana
mauretania-tingitana.summary: A Roman province in present-day northern Morocco, formed when the Kingdom of Mauretania was divided, with its capital at Tingis (Tangier).

africa-roman-province.name: Africa (Roman province)
africa-roman-province.summary: A Roman province on North Africa's coast, created in 146 BC after Rome's conquest of Carthage, covering roughly modern Tunisia and parts of Algeria and Libya; one of the empire's wealthiest provinces.

medjerda-river.name: Medjerda River
medjerda-river.summary: A 450-kilometre river, the longest in Tunisia, flowing from northeastern Algeria through Tunisia into the Gulf of Tunis; known in antiquity as the Bagradas.

mago-i-of-carthage.name: Mago I
mago-i-of-carthage.summary: King of Carthage from 550 to 530 BCE and founder of the Magonid dynasty, who rose from general to make Carthage the leading Phoenician power in the western Mediterranean.

magonids.name: Magonid dynasty
magonids.summary: A ruling dynasty of Carthage from 550 to 340 BCE, founded by Mago I, under which the Carthaginian empire expanded to include Sardinia, Libya and much of Sicily.

etruscan-civilization.name: Etruscans
etruscan-civilization.summary: A civilization of ancient Italy formed by a federation of city-states, with the earliest identifiably Etruscan culture dating from about 900 BC and its territory reaching its greatest extent around 500 BC.

tripolitania.name: Tripolitania
tripolitania.summary: A historic region of Libya settled since antiquity, ruled in turn by Carthage, Rome, the Vandals, the Byzantines, and Muslim and Ottoman conquerors by the 15th century.

battle-of-alalia.name: Battle of Alalia
battle-of-alalia.summary: A naval battle fought between 540 and 535 BC off Corsica, in which Greek Phocaeans defeated a larger allied Etruscan-Carthaginian fleet but at such cost that it ultimately benefited the Etruscans and Carthaginians.

huneric.name: Huneric
huneric.summary: King of the Vandals and Alans (r. 477-484), son of Gaiseric, who focused on internal affairs rather than his father's wider ambitions and was the first to use the title King of the Vandals and Alans.

gelimer.name: Gelimer
gelimer.summary: The last king of the Vandals in North Africa, reigning 530-534, whose defeat by the Byzantine general Belisarius in 533-534 ended the Vandal Kingdom.

majorian.name: Majorian
majorian.summary: Western Roman emperor from 457 to 461 who campaigned vigorously to recover imperial territory before being murdered in a conspiracy.

basiliscus.name: Basiliscus
basiliscus.summary: Eastern Roman emperor from 475 to 476, a general whose costly failed invasion of the Vandal Kingdom in 468 preceded his brief seizure of the throne from Zeno.

gaiseric.name: Gaiseric
gaiseric.summary: King of the Vandals and Alans (428–477) who captured and plundered Rome in 455 and turned the Vandals into a major Mediterranean power.

belisarius.name: Belisarius
belisarius.summary: A Byzantine military commander (c. 500-565) under Emperor Justinian I who reconquered North Africa and much of Italy, considered one of history's greatest generals.

cambyses-ii.name: Cambyses II
cambyses-ii.summary: Second king of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, ruling 530 to 522 BCE; son of Cyrus the Great, he conquered Egypt and Libya's coast before dying of a wound on his way home.

commodus.name: Commodus
commodus.summary: Roman emperor from 177 to 192, first as co-emperor with his father Marcus Aurelius, whose sole reign is often seen as ending the Pax Romana; he was assassinated in 192.

hispania-baetica.name: Baetica
hispania-baetica.summary: One of three Roman provinces created in Hispania (the Iberian Peninsula) in 27 BC, bordered by Lusitania and Tarraconensis; its territory roughly corresponds to modern Andalusia.

punic-religion.name: Punic religion
punic-religion.summary: The religion of Carthage and other western Phoenician settlements, continuing Canaanite religious traditions with local variations, surviving Rome's conquest into the fourth century AD in some places.

africa-goddess.name: Ifru
africa-goddess.summary: A Berber fertility and abundance goddess worshipped by the tribe of Ifri, depicted with an elephant-mask headdress, a cornucopia, a military standard and a lion.

melqart.name: Melqart
melqart.summary: The tutelary god of the Phoenician city of Tyre, linked to the founding of Phoenician colonies and later identified with the Greek Heracles and Roman Hercules.

marseille-tariff.name: Marseille Tariff
marseille-tariff.summary: A Punic-language inscription from the 3rd century BCE found at Marseille, thought to come from a temple of Baal Hammon in Carthage; one of the earliest and longest known Phoenician-alphabet inscriptions.

baal-zephon.name: Baal Saphon
baal-zephon.summary: An epithet of the Canaanite storm god Baal as lord of Mount Zaphon; sanctuaries in his honor were built around the Mediterranean by devotees seeking protection for maritime trade.

gammarth.name: Gammarth
gammarth.summary: A coastal town near Tunis, Tunisia, that grew from a fishing village into an upmarket seaside resort after independence from France.

djerba.name: Djerba
djerba.summary: Tunisian island in the Gulf of Gabès, the largest island in North Africa, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.

el-ghriba-synagogue.name: El Ghriba Synagogue
el-ghriba-synagogue.summary: An ancient synagogue on the Tunisian island of Djerba, possibly the oldest in the world, and a major Jewish pilgrimage site extensively renovated in the 19th century.

siege-of-jerusalem-597-bc.name: Siege of Jerusalem (597 BC)
siege-of-jerusalem-597-bc.summary: A 597 BC siege by Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon that forced Jerusalem's surrender and began the deportation of its king and elite to Babylon, marking the start of the Babylonian captivity.

tophet.name: Tophets
tophet.summary: Term archaeologists apply to open-air sanctuaries in Punic religion, including cemeteries at Carthaginian sites holding urns of cremated infants and animals, traditionally linked to child sacrifice.

serge-lancel.name: Serge Lancel
serge-lancel.summary: French archaeologist, historian and philologist who lived from 1928 to 2005.

byrsa.name: Byrsa
byrsa.summary: The walled citadel and hill overlooking the Phoenician harbour of ancient Carthage, Tunisia.

yennayer.name: Yennayer
yennayer.summary: The first month of the Berber (Amazigh) calendar, falling around 12-14 January; the calendar was created in 1980, dated from 950 BCE, and became an official holiday in Algeria in 2018 and Morocco in 2023.

shoshenq-i.name: Shoshenq I
shoshenq-i.summary: A pharaoh of ancient Egypt who reigned around 943–922 BC and founded the Twenty-second Dynasty, often identified with the Shishak named in the Hebrew Bible.
